script.title: HSA for freelancers: the triple tax break, with three real examples
script.hook: A health savings account is one of the few accounts with a tax break going in, while it grows, and coming out. For a long time most freelancers couldn't use one, because their marketplace plan didn't qualify. That changed in twenty twenty-six. In this video: who can open an HSA now, how much it saves three fictional freelancers, how it compares with an IRA, and the mistakes to avoid. Twenty twenty-six federal figures, education not advice.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: A health savings account is one of the few accounts with a tax break going in, while it grows, and coming out. For a long time most freelancers couldn't use one, because their marketplace plan didn't qualify. That changed in twenty twenty-six. In this video: who can open an HSA now, how much it saves three fictional freelancers, how it compares with an IRA, and the mistakes to avoid. Twenty twenty-six federal figures, education not advice.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes with a heart-shaped piggy bank. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Eligible
segments.narration: To put money into an HSA, you need to be covered by an HSA-eligible health plan, usually called a high-deductible health plan, and not have other disqualifying coverage, like a spouse's regular plan or Medicare. Being self-employed doesn't change any of that. The question is only which plan you have.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a health card with a checkmark. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: New rule
segments.narration: Here's the change. Starting in twenty twenty-six, bronze and catastrophic plans bought through the marketplace are treated as HSA-eligible. Before, many bronze plans didn't meet the technical rules. A lot of freelancers buy bronze plans to keep premiums down, so many of them can now open an HSA for the first time.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. three small cards, one highlighted. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Limits
segments.narration: For twenty twenty-six, you can contribute up to four thousand four hundred dollars with self-only coverage, or eight thousand seven hundred fifty with family coverage. If you're fifty-five or older, add a thousand. Twenty twenty-seven's limits are a little higher; check irs.gov. If you're only eligible part of the year, the limit is generally prorated by month.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two coin stacks. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Three
segments.narration: Three fictional freelancers, all single with self-only bronze plans, each putting in the full forty-four hundred. Mia expects thirty-five thousand of profit, Dev sixty thousand, Rosa a hundred thousand. How much federal tax does each one save this year?
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. three coin stacks. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Savings
segments.narration: Mia saves about three hundred sixty-seven dollars. Dev saves about four hundred twenty-two. Rosa saves about seven hundred seventy-four. The deduction cuts income tax but not self-employment tax, and the business income deduction shrinks a little with it, so the saving is a bit less than your bracket rate. With family coverage and the full eighty-seven fifty, the savings roughly double: about seven fifteen, eight forty, and fifteen forty.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. three bars rising. No text, no logos, no real people.

chart.title: Tax saved now by a $4,400 HSA

segments.heading: Grows
segments.narration: That's only the first tax break. Inside the HSA, the money can be invested, and growth isn't taxed. Then, when you take it out for qualified medical expenses, like doctor visits, prescriptions or dental work, it comes out tax-free. That's the triple tax break: deductible in, untaxed growth, tax-free out.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a small plant in a heart-shaped jar. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Any year
segments.narration: And there's no deadline to reimburse yourself. If you pay a medical bill out of pocket this year and keep the receipt, you can take that amount out of the HSA tax-free years later, as long as the expense happened after you opened the account. Some people use this on purpose, letting the HSA grow for decades.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a receipt in a folder. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Not FSA
segments.narration: Don't confuse it with an FSA. A flexible spending account is a workplace benefit with a use-it-or-lose-it rule. An HSA rolls over every year and belongs to you. If you change plans, stop freelancing or move, the money stays in your account.
segments.on_screen_text: Not an FSA: it rolls over
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a jar carried into a new year. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Deadline
segments.narration: Timing is generous. You can contribute for a year up to that year's tax filing deadline, usually mid-April. So you can wait until you know your profit, then decide. Report contributions on Form eight eight eight nine with your return.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a calendar with April circled. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Vs IRA
segments.narration: HSA or IRA first? If you qualify for an HSA and expect medical costs at some point, which almost everyone does, many people fill the HSA first. It's the only one that's tax-free on both ends for medical spending. After age sixty-five, HSA money can be taken out for anything, taxed like a traditional IRA if it isn't for medical costs.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two piggy banks, one heart-shaped. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Premiums
segments.narration: Your premiums are a separate break. As a freelancer, you can usually deduct your health insurance premiums as self-employed health insurance, up to your business profit, as long as you weren't eligible for an employer-subsidized plan, including through a spouse. That's on top of the HSA deduction.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a heart with a price tag. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Credits
segments.narration: One interaction to watch: premium tax credits on marketplace plans depend on your income. An HSA contribution lowers your modified adjusted gross income, which can raise your credit a little. If you get a credit, report changes in income to the marketplace during the year.
segments.on_screen_text: HSA can lower MAGI for credits
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a coin with a percent sign. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Mistakes
segments.narration: Four HSA mistakes. Contributing for months you weren't eligible, which creates an excess contribution with a six percent tax each year until fixed. Using it for non-medical costs before sixty-five, which means income tax plus a twenty percent penalty. Forgetting to invest it, so it sits as cash. And not keeping receipts for the medical expenses you pay from it.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. four small warning signs. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Open one
segments.narration: To open one, pick an HSA provider; many brokerages and banks offer them. Look for low fees and investment options. You don't have to use one tied to your insurer. Set up a monthly transfer, and keep the receipts for every medical bill in one folder.
segments.on_screen_text: Open one: low fees, invest it
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a laptop with a heart. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Bronze math
segments.narration: Is switching to a bronze plan worth it just for the HSA? Not automatically. A bronze plan has lower premiums but a higher deductible, so you pay more when you need care. Compare the premium difference for a year, plus the HSA tax saving, against the extra you could pay out of pocket in a bad year. If you rarely see a doctor, bronze plus an HSA often comes out ahead. If you have ongoing care, run the numbers carefully.
segments.on_screen_text: Bronze + HSA: compare the whole cost
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two bars with a heart. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Family
segments.narration: With family coverage, the limit roughly doubles, and so does the value. A couple where one spouse freelances and the family is on a bronze marketplace plan can put in up to eight thousand seven hundred fifty for twenty twenty-six. If both spouses are fifty-five or older, each can add a thousand catch-up, but it has to go into each person's own HSA.

segments.heading: Spouse plan
segments.narration: If your spouse has a regular, non-HSA plan through work that also covers you, you generally can't contribute to an HSA, even if you buy your own bronze plan. The other coverage disqualifies you. Check what you're actually enrolled in before you open an account.
segments.on_screen_text: Covered by a spouse's regular plan? No HSA
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a heart with a lock. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Investing
segments.narration: Investing it: most HSA providers let you keep a small cash amount for near-term bills and invest the rest in funds. If you can pay current medical costs from your regular budget and save the receipts, the invested money has years to grow, and you can reimburse yourself later, tax-free.
segments.on_screen_text: Keep some cash, invest the rest

segments.heading: Records
segments.narration: Keep three records: your contributions, with dates; every distribution, and the medical expense it paid for; and the receipts. The HSA provider sends Form 1099-SA for distributions and Form 5498-SA for contributions. You report both on Form 8889.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a folder with two forms. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Not eligible
segments.narration: If you can't use an HSA, because your plan isn't eligible or you have other coverage, the next best options are the self-employed health insurance deduction for your premiums, and a traditional or Roth IRA for long-term saving. Medical costs above a share of your income may be deductible if you itemize, but most freelancers take the standard deduction.

segments.narration: Open enrollment for twenty twenty-eight starts November first. If you want an HSA next year, check that the plan you pick is marked HSA-eligible on healthcare.gov or your state's marketplace before you enroll.

script.title: Quitting your job to freelance: the numbers to run first
script.hook: Thinking about leaving a salaried job to freelance full-time? The question most people ask is whether they can find enough clients. The question that sinks more people is whether they priced in everything the employer used to pay. In this video we'll follow one fictional person from a seventy-thousand-dollar salary to the freelance profit, revenue and hourly rate it takes to come out even, then cover runway, health insurance and the first-year tax trap. Twenty twenty-six federal figures, education not advice.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: Thinking about leaving a salaried job to freelance full-time? The question most people ask is whether they can find enough clients. The question that sinks more people is whether they priced in everything the employer used to pay. In this video we'll follow one fictional person from a seventy-thousand-dollar salary to the freelance profit, revenue and hourly rate it takes to come out even, then cover runway, health insurance and the first-year tax trap. Twenty twenty-six federal figures, education not advice.
segments.on_screen_text: Quitting to freelance: run the numbers
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes with a briefcase and a laptop. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Morgan
segments.narration: Meet Morgan, fictional, a marketing manager earning seventy thousand dollars. The employer pays most of the health insurance and matches three percent into a 401(k). Morgan wants to freelance doing the same work for former clients and agencies.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes next to a paycheck. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Take-home
segments.narration: First, what does Morgan actually keep now? Federal income tax on seventy thousand of wages, single, is about sixty-five hundred seventy. Morgan's share of Social Security and Medicare, seven point six five percent, is about fifty-three fifty-five. That leaves about fifty-eight thousand seventy-five after federal taxes, before state tax. That's the number to match.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a coin stack with two slices taken. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Payroll
segments.narration: As a freelancer, Morgan pays both halves of Social Security and Medicare, as self-employment tax: fifteen point three percent on most of the profit. Half of it comes back as a deduction, and there's the twenty percent business income deduction, but the net effect is that each dollar of profit is taxed more than a dollar of salary was at the bottom.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two coins where there was one. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Match profit
segments.narration: If the only goal were matching fifty-eight thousand seventy-five after federal tax, Morgan would need about seventy-three thousand one fifty of profit. But two other costs move over too.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a coin stack. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Benefits
segments.narration: Health insurance: say Morgan's own plan costs six thousand a year. As a freelancer, that's usually deductible as self-employed health insurance, which helps. Retirement: the three percent match was worth twenty-one hundred a year, and Morgan would have to save that from profit. Add both, and Morgan needs about eighty-two thousand nine hundred twenty of profit to come out even.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a heart and a piggy bank. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Chart
segments.narration: Side by side: seventy thousand of salary. About eighty-two thousand nine hundred of freelance profit to match it. Add five thousand of business costs, like software, a laptop and insurance, and that's about eighty-seven thousand nine hundred of revenue. Twenty-five percent more than the salary, just to stand still.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. three bars rising. No text, no logos, no real people.

chart.title: What it takes to replace a $70K salary
chart.note: 2026 federal, single. Includes health premiums and a 3% match. Fictional.

segments.heading: Rate
segments.narration: Now the hourly rate. A salaried job pays for about two thousand hours. A freelancer bills far fewer, because of finding clients, admin and time off. A thousand billable hours a year is realistic for many. Eighty-seven thousand nine hundred divided by a thousand is about eighty-eight dollars an hour. At fifteen hundred hours, about fifty-nine.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a clock. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Runway
segments.narration: Next, runway. The first months usually earn less than the target. Add up a month of personal spending, multiply by at least six, and add the first few months of health insurance. If you don't have clients lined up, aim for more. Keep it in its own account, not mixed with future tax money.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a small plane on a runway. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Health
segments.narration: Health insurance when you leave. Losing job-based coverage generally opens a sixty-day special enrollment period on the marketplace, where premium tax credits depend on your expected income. Or you can elect COBRA and keep your work plan, usually at the full cost plus a fee, for up to eighteen months. Compare the total cost, including the deductible.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a heart with a clock. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 401k
segments.narration: Your old 401(k). You can usually leave it where it is, roll it into an IRA, or into a Solo 401(k) later. Cashing it out is the expensive option: income tax plus, generally, a ten percent additional tax if you're under fifty-nine and a half. Then open your own retirement account once the business has profit.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a piggy bank with an arrow. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: First year tax
segments.narration: The first-year tax trap. In your first year, there's often no estimated payment required to avoid the penalty if your previous year's withholding covered last year's tax. But the tax on your freelance profit is still due in April. Set aside a share of every payment from day one, so April isn't a shock.
segments.on_screen_text: Year one: save even if no penalty
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a jar with a line. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Mid-year
segments.narration: Leaving mid-year? Your W-2 withholding for the months you worked counts toward this year's tax, and it's treated as paid evenly through the year. That can cover much of the first partial year. Run the IRS Tax Withholding Estimator or our calculator to check what's left.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. four equal coins. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Side first
segments.narration: Many people reduce the risk by starting on the side. Keep the job, take a couple of freelance clients, and see whether the rate and demand are real. Your W-2 withholding can cover the side income's tax with a new W-4. Then quit once the side income covers a good share of your target.
segments.on_screen_text: Test it on the side first
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a laptop next to a briefcase. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Checklist
segments.narration: Before your last day: runway saved, a health plan picked, a plan for the old 401(k), business and tax savings accounts open, a free EIN from irs.gov, and your rate worked out with a calculator, not a guess. And ideally, a first client or two signed.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a clipboard with checkmarks. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Time
segments.narration: Count your time, not just your rate. As an employee, Morgan was paid for holidays and vacation. As a freelancer, a two-week vacation is two weeks with no billing, and so are sick days, admin, sales calls and learning. That's why the thousand-hour figure isn't pessimistic. Track your billable hours from the first month and adjust your rate if they come in lower.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a beach umbrella and a clock. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Pipeline
segments.narration: The best predictor of a smooth first year is having work lined up before you leave. A former employer as a first client, agencies that already know you, or two or three side clients who will take more of your time. Ask before you resign, and get the first one in writing with a deposit.
segments.on_screen_text: Line up work before you leave
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. three small arrows. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Equipment
segments.narration: Equipment and software that the employer provided now come out of your budget: a laptop, design or office software, a phone, maybe a coworking membership. They're business expenses, so they lower your profit and your tax, but they still cost cash in month one. Put them in the runway.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a laptop with a price tag. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Mid-year math
segments.narration: If Morgan leaves in July, the year splits in two. Six months of salary with withholding, then six months of freelance profit with none. The withholding counts as paid evenly through the year, so it can cover a good part of the year's total. Run both halves through a calculator in July and again in October.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a calendar split in two. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: State
segments.narration: Remember state tax too. A state with an income tax will tax the freelance profit, and most expect estimated payments on similar dates. Add a few percent of profit to the set-aside, depending on your state.
segments.on_screen_text: Add state tax to the plan
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a map outline with a coin. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Unemployment
segments.narration: One more difference: unemployment insurance. In most states, self-employed people aren't covered, so if freelance work dries up, there's no state benefit to fall back on. That's why the runway and, later, an emergency fund matter more than they did as an employee.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. an umbrella with a hole. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Paperwork
segments.narration: Paperwork you'll suddenly own: invoices, contracts, W-9s for clients, 1099s in January, quarterly payments, and a Schedule C at tax time. Budget an hour a week for it from the start, or the cost of a bookkeeper or tax preparer in your business costs.
segments.on_screen_text: An hour a week for admin
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a clipboard. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Calculator
segments.narration: Want your own numbers? The free rate calculator in the link in bio starts from the take-home you want and works back through taxes, costs and billable hours, the same way we did for Morgan.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a calculator. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Recap. A seventy-thousand-dollar salary kept Morgan about fifty-eight thousand after federal tax. To match it after paying both halves of payroll tax, health insurance and a retirement match, Morgan needs about eighty-three thousand of profit, eighty-eight thousand of revenue, or about eighty-eight dollars an hour at a thousand billable hours. Build six months of runway, choose health coverage within sixty days, don't cash out the 401(k), and save for April from day one. Subscribe for one freelancer money move a week.

script.title: Creator taxes: brand deals, gifted products and the gear you can deduct
script.hook: If you make money from content, as a YouTuber, streamer, podcaster or influencer, you're running a small business in the eyes of the IRS, whether you think of it that way or not. In this video: what counts as income, including the free products brands send you, which expenses you can deduct, the forms you will and won't get, and what one fictional creator owes. Twenty twenty-six federal figures, education not advice.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: If you make money from content, as a YouTuber, streamer, podcaster or influencer, you're running a small business in the eyes of the IRS, whether you think of it that way or not. In this video: what counts as income, including the free products brands send you, which expenses you can deduct, the forms you will and won't get, and what one fictional creator owes. Twenty twenty-six federal figures, education not advice.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes with a camera. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Remy
segments.narration: Meet Remy, a fictional lifestyle creator. This year Remy earned thirty thousand dollars from brand deals, six thousand of platform payouts and ad revenue, and received about two thousand dollars of products from brands in exchange for posts. Remy spent nine thousand on gear, software, an editor and the business share of a phone.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes with a camera and a laptop. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Business
segments.narration: First question: hobby or business? If you're doing it to make a profit, keep records and act like a business, you're a business, and you report income and expenses on Schedule C. If it's a hobby, the income is still reportable, but you can't deduct the costs. For anyone earning real money from content, being treated as a business is usually better.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a form with a small camera. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Income types
segments.narration: Every kind of creator income counts: brand deals and sponsorships, platform payouts and ad revenue, affiliate commissions, tips and memberships, and merch sales. It doesn't matter whether it arrives by bank transfer, PayPal or a platform's own system.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. five small icons in a row. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Gifted
segments.narration: Gifted products are the one people miss. When a brand sends you something in exchange for a post, a video or a review, the fair market value is generally income, just as if they'd paid you cash. Remy's two thousand dollars of products count. Something sent with no expectation at all is less clear. Keep a log of everything you receive, with its value and whether content was expected.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a gift box with a price tag. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Forms
segments.narration: The forms. A brand that paid you two thousand dollars or more in twenty twenty-six should send a 1099-NEC. Payment apps and some platforms send a 1099-K once you pass twenty thousand dollars and two hundred transactions. Many smaller payments come with no form. None of that changes what's reportable. Your own log is the real source.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. three forms, one blank. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Deductions
segments.narration: Now deductions. Common ones for creators: cameras, microphones and lights; editing software and subscriptions; props and supplies used only for content; editors, designers and other contractors; and the business share of your phone and internet. Costs to set up a home studio may fit the home office rules if that space is used regularly and only for the business.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a camera, a laptop and a phone. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Business share
segments.narration: The business-use rule matters most for creators, because so much of what you film with is also personal. A phone used half for content is about half deductible. A camera used only for content is fully deductible. Keep a simple note of how you worked out each percentage.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a phone split in half. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Not deductible
segments.narration: What generally isn't deductible: everyday clothes, even if you wear them on camera, unless they aren't suitable for everyday wear; personal trips, even if you post from them; and gym memberships. A trip that's mainly for a brand shoot or a conference has its own travel rules.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a shirt with a cross. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Remy's tax
segments.narration: Back to Remy. Income: thirty thousand, plus six thousand, plus two thousand of products: thirty-eight thousand. Minus nine thousand of costs: twenty-nine thousand of profit. Self-employment tax is about four thousand ninety-eight. Income tax, after the standard deduction and the business income deduction, is about eight sixty-eight. Total federal: about four thousand nine hundred sixty-six, about seventeen percent of profit.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a coin stack with a slice. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Breakdown
segments.narration: Look at the split: the self-employment tax is almost five times the income tax. That's typical at this level, and it surprises creators who expect a low bracket to mean a low bill. Self-employment tax starts with the first dollar of profit.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two bars, one much taller. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Quarterly
segments.narration: Because no tax is withheld from creator income, Remy is expected to pay quarterly estimated taxes once the year's tax is a thousand dollars or more. At about forty-nine sixty-six, that's roughly twelve forty a quarter. Brand deals tend to be lumpy, so set aside twenty-five to thirty percent of every payment the day it lands.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. four calendar pages. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Setup
segments.narration: A simple creator setup: a separate business bank account for all creator money; a free EIN from irs.gov, so brands don't need your Social Security number on their W-9s; a brand-deal log with cash and product values; a folder of receipts; and a tax savings account.
segments.on_screen_text: Account, EIN, log, receipts, tax jar
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a small row of jars and a folder. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: State
segments.narration: Don't forget state tax. Most states with an income tax treat creator income like any other business income. Some states also want sales tax on merch you sell, and a few on certain digital products. Check your state's revenue site before you launch a store.
segments.on_screen_text: State tax, and maybe sales tax
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a map outline with a coin. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Mistakes
segments.narration: Five creator tax mistakes. Ignoring gifted products. Waiting for 1099s that never come. Deducting a hundred percent of a personal phone. Spending brand-deal money before setting the tax share aside. And mixing creator income into a personal account, which makes all of the above harder.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. five small warning signs. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Home studio
segments.narration: A home studio can qualify for the home office deduction if the space is used regularly and only for the business. A corner of the bedroom that's also where you sleep doesn't qualify. A spare room used only for filming and editing can. The simplified method is five dollars a square foot, up to three hundred square feet.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a small room with a camera. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Travel
segments.narration: Travel for content. A trip whose main purpose is business, like a brand shoot or a creator conference, can have deductible travel costs, with meals generally at fifty percent. A vacation where you also post doesn't become a business trip. Keep the brand agreement or conference schedule as proof of purpose.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a suitcase with a camera. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Merch
segments.narration: Selling merch or digital products adds a second kind of business inside your channel: cost of goods, platform fees, and sometimes state sales tax. Track merch sales separately in your log, so you can see what each one actually earns after costs.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a small t-shirt with a tag. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Brand contracts
segments.narration: Brand contracts often say who pays for what. If a brand reimburses your travel, that reimbursement may be income, and the costs deductible. If they ship you equipment to keep, that's income at its value. Read the payment terms with taxes in mind.
segments.on_screen_text: Read brand contracts for tax terms
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a contract with a coin. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Foreign brands
segments.narration: Paid by a brand outside the US? It's still income on Schedule C, reported in US dollars, usually with no 1099. If they ask for a tax form, a US creator gives a W-9, not a W-8BEN.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a globe with a camera. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Age
segments.narration: Young creators: a minor who earns money from content can owe self-employment tax once net earnings reach four hundred dollars, and may need to file a return even if they're a dependent. Parents managing a child's channel should keep the child's income and records separate.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a small figure with a camera. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Payment apps
segments.narration: Brand payments through payment apps sometimes come labeled as goods and services, which can trigger a 1099-K. Personal transfers from friends and family aren't income. Keep business and personal payments on separate accounts so the forms make sense.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a phone with two coins. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Pro help
segments.narration: When to get a tax professional: your first year with real income, a big jump in revenue, a move to another state, or forming an LLC or S corp. One good appointment can set up your categories and quarterly plan for years.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a speech bubble with a question mark. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Recap. If you create for profit, you're a business: report all of it on Schedule C, including products you got in exchange for content. Deduct gear, software and help, but only the business share of things you also use personally. Expect self-employment tax to be most of the bill: about forty-nine sixty-six on Remy's twenty-nine thousand of profit. Pay quarterly, keep a brand-deal log, and set aside twenty-five to thirty percent. Subscribe for one freelancer money move a week.

script.title: How big should a freelancer's emergency fund be? Three real examples
script.hook: Employees are usually told to keep three to six months of expenses saved. For freelancers, that advice is often too thin, because your income can drop to zero with no notice, and there's no unemployment check in most cases. In this video: how to size a freelance emergency fund, three fictional examples, where to keep it, how to build it without starving your tax account, and when to use it. Education, not advice.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: Employees are usually told to keep three to six months of expenses saved. For freelancers, that advice is often too thin, because your income can drop to zero with no notice, and there's no unemployment check in most cases. In this video: how to size a freelance emergency fund, three fictional examples, where to keep it, how to build it without starving your tax account, and when to use it. Education, not advice.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes with three jars. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Different
segments.narration: Why different? An employee who loses a job often gets a final paycheck, maybe severance, and can usually apply for unemployment. A freelancer who loses a big client gets none of that, and still has a quarterly tax payment due on the old income. Income can be lumpy even in a good year.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. an empty mailbox. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Count
segments.narration: Start with the right number: personal spending, not business costs. Rent or mortgage, food, insurance including health, debt payments, transport and the basics. Don't include taxes on income you haven't earned yet, or business costs you'd cut if work dried up. For our examples, say three thousand five hundred dollars a month.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a receipt. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Rule
segments.narration: A simple rule of thumb. Six months of personal spending if your income is steady: several clients and some retainers. Nine months if it's project-based and lumpy. Twelve months if one client is most of your income, or you're the sole earner with dependents. These are planning guides, not rules.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. three jars of different sizes. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Avery
segments.narration: Example one, fictional: Avery, a bookkeeper with eight monthly retainer clients. Income barely moves month to month, and losing one client is a twelve percent dip, not a cliff. Six months: twenty-one thousand dollars.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. six coins. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Jules
segments.narration: Example two: Jules, a video editor paid by the project. Some months bring twelve thousand, others two. Nine months: thirty-one thousand five hundred.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. nine coins. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Robin
segments.narration: Example three: Robin, a developer with one large client paying seventy percent of the bills. Good money, high risk: if that contract ends, Robin needs time to replace most of the income. Twelve months: forty-two thousand.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. twelve coins. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Chart
segments.narration: Side by side: twenty-one thousand, thirty-one thousand five hundred and forty-two thousand, for the same monthly spending. The difference isn't how much each person earns. It's how fragile the income is.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. three bars rising. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Three pots
segments.narration: Keep three pots separate. Tax savings is already owed to the IRS, so it never counts as emergency money. A salary buffer, a month or two of pay in the business account, smooths normal ups and downs. The emergency fund is for the unexpected: a lost client, an illness, a broken laptop the week of a deadline.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. three jars with walls between. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Where
segments.narration: Where to keep it: a separate savings account, insured by the FDIC at a bank, or the equivalent at a credit union, that you can reach within a day or two. Not the stock market, which can drop just when you need it. Compare a few savings rates, because the difference on thirty thousand dollars adds up.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a jar with a shield. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Build
segments.narration: Building it takes time, and that's fine. A simple order: tax money first, every payment. Then a small fixed share, even five percent, of every client payment into the emergency fund. Put windfalls, like a big project or a tax refund, straight in. Jules saving five percent of sixty thousand a year adds three thousand a year, plus windfalls.
segments.on_screen_text: Tax first, then 5% of every payment
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a small coin going into a jar. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Milestones
segments.narration: Use milestones so it doesn't feel endless. One month first, then three, then the full target. One month alone means a late invoice no longer touches your tax savings. Three months covers most short gaps.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a staircase. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: When
segments.narration: When to use it: a real loss of income, a medical bill, an essential repair or replacement for the business. When not to: a vacation, a planned purchase, or this quarter's estimated tax. If you do use it, cut spending and refill it before anything else after taxes.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a jar with a small lock. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Insurance
segments.narration: An emergency fund isn't the only protection. Disability insurance replaces part of your income if you can't work for a long time. Health insurance keeps a medical emergency from emptying the fund. For a freelancer with dependents, term life insurance is worth a look too.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a shield and a heart. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Taxes
segments.narration: One tax note: if your income drops for the rest of the year, your estimated payments based on this year's income can drop too. Re-project before the next payment. If you use last year's tax as your safe harbor, the payment stays the same, so keep that in your plan.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a calendar with a smaller coin. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Start date
segments.narration: When should you start? Before you go freelance, ideally. If you're already freelancing without one, start now, even small. One month of spending sitting in its own account changes how a late invoice feels.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a calendar with a coin. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Debt
segments.narration: Debt or emergency fund first? A common approach is a small starter fund, like one month, then extra payments on high-interest debt, then the rest of the fund. Without any cushion, the next surprise goes straight back on the card.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a jar and a card. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Couples
segments.narration: If you share expenses with a partner who has steady W-2 income, your household fund can often be smaller, because one income is stable. Size it on the household's spending and what would happen if the freelance income dropped to zero for a few months.
segments.on_screen_text: Couples: size it on the household
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two rings and a jar. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Seasonal
segments.narration: Seasonal freelancers, like wedding photographers or tax preparers, know their slow months in advance. That's a planning problem more than an emergency. Put the slow-season pay into the salary buffer, and keep the emergency fund for true surprises.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a calendar with a dip. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Review
segments.narration: Review the target once a year, or after a big change: a new big client, a move, a new child, or a rise in rent. The target follows your spending and your risk, not your income.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a magnifying glass. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Late invoices
segments.narration: Late invoices are the most common freelance emergency, and the cheapest to prevent. Deposits, clear payment terms and a polite reminder schedule shrink how often you need the fund. Our contract checklist and invoice template are in the link in bio.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. an invoice with a clock. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Health costs
segments.narration: Health costs are the other big one. With a high-deductible plan, keep at least the deductible available, in the emergency fund or an HSA. That way a medical bill doesn't turn into a credit card balance.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a heart with a coin. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Equipment
segments.narration: For a freelancer, a broken laptop can mean lost income on top of the repair. Some people keep a small equipment line inside the fund, or a backup device, so a breakdown costs a day, not a week.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a laptop with a crack. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Check-in
segments.narration: A quick quarterly check: is the fund at target? Did you use any of it? Has your spending changed? Do it on the same day as your estimated tax payment, so it becomes part of the routine.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a calendar with four marks. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Feeling
segments.narration: And the part that's hard to put in a spreadsheet: a full emergency fund changes how you work. You can turn down a bad-fit client, negotiate rates calmly, and take a week off when you need it. For many freelancers, that freedom is the real return.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes relaxing with a jar. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Taxes owed
segments.narration: One more case: a big tax bill you didn't plan for, say after a much better year than expected. That's what the tax savings account and the safe harbor are for. If you're short, an IRS payment plan usually costs less than draining the emergency fund to zero. Keep at least one month in reserve either way.
segments.on_screen_text: Short on tax? Payment plan first
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a calendar with small coins. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Recap. Size a freelance emergency fund on personal spending: six months if your income is steady, nine if it's lumpy, twelve if one client dominates. At thirty-five hundred a month, that's twenty-one thousand, thirty-one thousand five hundred or forty-two thousand. Keep it separate from tax money and your salary buffer, insured and easy to reach. Build it with a fixed share of every payment and windfalls, and refill it first after you use it. Subscribe for one freelancer money move a week.

No text, no logos, no real people.
